question: According to the manual, what portion of truck driver deaths in crashes result from truck rollovers?
choice_a: More than half
choice_b: About one quarter
choice_c: Nearly all
choice_d: Less than 10 percent
explanation: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: How much more likely are fully loaded rigs to roll over in a crash compared to empty rigs?
choice_a: Twice as likely
choice_b: Five times as likely
choice_c: They are equally likely
choice_d: Ten times as likely
explanation: Fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs, since piled-up cargo raises the vehicle's center of gravity.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: What two things does the manual say will help prevent rollover?
choice_a: Driving faster and braking harder
choice_b: Loading cargo to one side and using the trailer hand valve often
choice_c: Keeping tires overinflated and using cruise control
choice_d: Keeping the cargo as close to the ground as possible and driving slowly around turns
explanation: Keeping the cargo as close to the ground as possible and driving slowly around turns are the two things that help prevent rollover; cargo should also be kept centered and spread out.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: What causes the dangerous 'crack-the-whip' effect in trucks pulling trailers?
choice_a: Rearward amplification during a quick lane change
choice_b: Slow, gradual steering inputs
choice_c: Using the trailer hand valve while parking
choice_d: Draining the air tanks too often
explanation: Rearward amplification causes the crack-the-whip effect; a quick lane change can turn the trailer over, with many accidents involving only the trailer overturning.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.2, Steer Gently

question: What does a rearward amplification value of 3.5 for triples mean?
choice_a: The vehicle can carry 3.5 times more cargo safely
choice_b: It refers to the number of axles allowed
choice_c: The last trailer can be rolled 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor
choice_d: Stopping distance is reduced by 3.5 times
explanation: Rearward amplification of 3.5 for triples means the last trailer can be rolled 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor, since triples have the greatest crack-the-whip effect of the combination types discussed.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.2, Steer Gently

question: What following distance rule does the manual suggest when pulling trailers?
choice_a: At least 1 car length per 10 mph
choice_b: At least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph
choice_c: A fixed 2 seconds regardless of vehicle length or speed
choice_d: No specific following distance is recommended
explanation: Drivers should follow far enough behind other vehicles, at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph, and look far enough ahead to avoid sudden lane changes.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.2, Steer Gently

question: Why do large combination vehicles often take longer to stop when empty than when fully loaded?
choice_a: Empty trailers weigh more than loaded ones
choice_b: Empty vehicles have weaker brakes installed
choice_c: The tractor protection valve does not function when empty
choice_d: The very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction, making it easy to lock up the wheels
explanation: When lightly loaded, the very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and make it very easy to lock up the wheels, which can cause the trailer to swing out or the tractor to jackknife quickly.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.3, Brake Early

question: What does the manual say about stopping a 'bobtail' tractor (a tractor without a semitrailer)?
choice_a: Bobtails are exempt from following distance rules
choice_b: Bobtails always stop faster than any loaded rig
choice_c: Bobtails cannot use air brakes
choice_d: Bobtails can be very hard to stop smoothly and take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight
explanation: Tests have shown that bobtail tractors can be very hard to stop smoothly and take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight, so drivers must be very careful driving bobtail.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.3, Brake Early

question: What type of trailers are most likely to get stuck on raised railroad-highway crossings?
choice_a: Refrigerated vans
choice_b: Tanker trailers only
choice_c: Standard flatbed trailers with high ground clearance
choice_d: Low slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, or possum-belly livestock trailers
explanation: Low slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers, and single-axle tractors pulling long trailers with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor, can get stuck on raised railroad crossings.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.4, Railroad-highway Crossings

question: If a vehicle gets stuck on railroad tracks, what should the driver do first?
choice_a: Stay in the vehicle and wait for a train to pass
choice_b: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then check for emergency notification information and call 911
choice_c: Try to free the vehicle by rocking it back and forth for several minutes
choice_d: Immediately attempt to uncouple the trailer
explanation: If stuck on the tracks, the driver should get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, check signposts or signal housing at the crossing for emergency notification information, and call 911 or another emergency number, giving the crossing's location and DOT number if posted.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.4, Railroad-highway Crossings

question: What is the best and earliest way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: By listening for the low air pressure buzzer
choice_b: By checking the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: By feeling a vibration in the steering wheel
choice_d: By seeing it in your mirrors
explanation: The earliest and best way to recognize that the trailer has started to skid is by seeing it in your mirrors; once the trailer swings out of the lane, it becomes very difficult to prevent a jackknife.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.5, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is the correct way to stop a trailer skid ('trailer jackknife')?
choice_a: Use the trailer hand brake to straighten out the rig
choice_b: Accelerate sharply to pull the trailer straight
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel hard in the opposite direction of the skid
choice_d: Release the brakes to regain traction; once the trailer wheels grip the road again, it will follow the tractor and straighten out
explanation: The driver should release the brakes to get traction back and should not use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out the rig, since the trailer wheel brakes caused the skid in the first place; once the trailer wheels grip the road again, the trailer will follow the tractor and straighten out.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.5, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is 'off-tracking' (or 'cheating') in a combination vehicle?
choice_a: When the driver crosses the air lines during coupling
choice_b: When the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels as the vehicle goes around a corner
choice_c: When the tractor protection valve fails to close
choice_d: When the trailer brakes are out of adjustment
explanation: Off-tracking, or 'cheating,' occurs when the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels as a vehicle goes around a corner; this causes the path followed by a tractor to be wider than the rig itself, and longer vehicles off-track more.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.6, Turn Wide

question: When turning a corner, why should a driver steer the front end wide while keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb, rather than swinging wide to the left before starting the turn?
choice_a: It is required for the fifth wheel to lock properly
choice_b: It reduces fuel consumption
choice_c: It prevents the ABS malfunction lamp from lighting up
choice_d: It keeps other drivers from passing on the right during the turn
explanation: If a driver cannot complete a turn without entering another lane, turning wide as the turn is completed (rather than swinging wide to the left before starting) is better because it keeps other drivers from passing on the right.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.6, Turn Wide

question: When backing a trailer, which direction should the driver turn the top of the steering wheel to make the trailer go in a desired direction?
choice_a: It does not matter which way the wheel is turned
choice_b: Only left, regardless of the desired direction
choice_c: The opposite direction from when backing a car, then the other way once the trailer starts to turn
choice_d: The same direction as when backing a car
explanation: When backing a car, straight truck, or bus, the driver turns the top of the wheel in the direction they want to go; when backing a trailer, the driver turns the wheel in the opposite direction, then must turn the wheel the other way once the trailer starts to turn to follow it.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: If a driver must back a trailer on a curved path, to which side should they back?
choice_a: The passenger's side, so a helper can guide them
choice_b: It does not matter which side
choice_c: Directly forward is always required instead
choice_d: The driver's side, so they can see
explanation: Whenever possible, a driver should position the vehicle to back in a straight line; if backing on a curved path is necessary, they should back to the driver's side so they can see.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: What backing technique helps a driver make corrections before getting too far off course?
choice_a: Backing as fast as possible
choice_b: Backing slowly
choice_c: Backing with the parking brake engaged
choice_d: Backing only in a straight line, never checking mirrors
explanation: Backing slowly lets the driver make corrections before getting too far off course; drivers should also use mirrors on both sides frequently and correct drift immediately by turning the top of the wheel in the direction of the drift.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: What is the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) supposed to be used for?
choice_a: To release the tractor protection valve
choice_b: Only to test the trailer brakes, not for driving
choice_c: To drain the trailer air tanks
choice_d: As the primary brake control during normal driving
explanation: The trailer hand valve works the trailer brakes and should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not in driving, because of the danger of making the trailer skid; the foot brake sends air to all the brakes with much less danger of causing a skid or jackknife.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.1, Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should the trailer hand valve never be used for parking?
choice_a: It disconnects the electrical cord
choice_b: It uses too much fuel
choice_c: It automatically engages the ABS system
choice_d: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers without spring brakes
explanation: The hand valve should never be used for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes on trailers that don't have spring brakes; the parking brakes should always be used when parking, with wheel chocks if the trailer lacks spring brakes.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.1, Trailer Hand Valve

question: What is the purpose of the tractor protection valve?
choice_a: To lubricate the fifth wheel
choice_b: To increase the governor cut-out pressure
choice_c: To control the ABS malfunction lamps
choice_d: To keep air in the tractor or truck brake system if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak
explanation: The tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak; it is controlled by the trailer air supply control valve in the cab.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.2, Tractor Protection Valve

question: At about what air pressure range will the tractor protection valve close automatically?
choice_a: 100 to 125 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi
choice_c: 55 to 80 psi
choice_d: 0 to 10 psi
explanation: The tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi; when it closes, it stops air from leaving the tractor and lets air out of the trailer emergency line, causing the trailer emergency brakes to come on.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.2, Tractor Protection Valve

question: On newer vehicles, what does the red eight-sided trailer air supply control knob do?
choice_a: Pulled out it supplies air; pushed in it shuts the air off
choice_b: It controls the windshield washer fluid
choice_c: It only operates the parking brake on the tractor
choice_d: Pushed in it supplies the trailer with air; pulled out it shuts the air off and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
explanation: The trailer air supply control on newer vehicles is a red eight-sided knob; the driver pushes it in to supply the trailer with air and pulls it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes. It will also pop out automatically when air pressure drops into the 20 to 45 psi range.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.3, Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What are the two air-lines that run between vehicles in a combination rig?
choice_a: The parking line and the driving line
choice_b: The primary line and the secondary line
choice_c: The intake line and the exhaust line
choice_d: The service line and the emergency line
explanation: Every combination vehicle has two air-lines: the service line (also called the control or signal line) and the emergency line (also called the supply line), running between each unit of the combination.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.4, Trailer Air-lines

question: What does the emergency (supply) line do in a combination vehicle's air brake system?
choice_a: It has no connection to the trailer's brakes
choice_b: It is only used when connecting the electrical cord
choice_c: It only carries electrical signals for the brake lights
choice_d: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes; losing pressure in it causes the trailer emergency brakes to come on
explanation: The emergency line supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles; a loss of air pressure in the emergency line, such as from a trailer breaking loose, causes the trailer emergency brakes to come on.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.4, Trailer Air-lines

question: What color is the emergency air-line typically coded to avoid confusion with the service line?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Blue
choice_c: Green
choice_d: Yellow
explanation: Emergency lines are often coded with the color red (red hose, red couplers, or other parts) to keep from getting them mixed up with the blue service line.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.4, Trailer Air-lines

question: How should glad hands be connected?
choice_a: Connect them only after the trailer is already moving
choice_b: Press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other, then turn to join and lock the couplers
choice_c: Twist them 360 degrees before connecting
choice_d: Simply push the couplers straight together without turning
explanation: When connecting glad hands, the driver should press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other; a turn of the glad hand attached to the hose will join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.5, Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What could happen if you cross the air-lines when coupling a trailer?
choice_a: Nothing significant would happen
choice_b: The alcohol evaporator would overfill
choice_c: The governor cut-out pressure would automatically increase
choice_d: Supply air would go to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so spring brakes might not release and older trailers could have no emergency brakes
explanation: If the air-lines are crossed, supply air is sent to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks; air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes, and on older trailers without spring brakes, there would be no emergency brakes and the wheels could turn freely, which is very dangerous.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.6, Trailer Air Tanks

question: When towing more than one trailer, how should the shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back of the trailers be positioned?
choice_a: All shut-off valves should be closed
choice_b: It does not matter as long as the engine is running
choice_c: Only the valve on the first trailer should be open
choice_d: All shut-off valves should be open except the one at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed
explanation: Shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) allow closing off the air-lines when another trailer is not being towed; the driver must check that all shut-off valves are open except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.7, Shut-off Valves

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Why is it especially important to use wheel chocks when parking trailers without spring brakes?
choice_a: Because it prevents the ABS malfunction lamp from illuminating
choice_b: Because chocks are legally required on every trailer regardless of brake type
choice_c: Because these trailers rely on air stored in the trailer air tank for emergency brakes, and the air will eventually leak away, leaving no brakes
choice_d: Because it eliminates the need for the parking brake control knob
explanation: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes; those without spring brakes have emergency brakes that work from air stored in the trailer air tank, and since that air will eventually leak away leaving no brakes, wheel chocks are very important for safety when parking these trailers.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.2.8, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: All trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: March 1, 1994
choice_d: March 1, 2000
explanation: All trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have ABS, though many built before that date have been voluntarily equipped with it.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Where are the ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers?
choice_a: On the right side of the trailer only
choice_b: On the instrument panel inside the cab
choice_c: Underneath the trailer, not visible from outside
choice_d: On the left side, either the front or rear corner of the trailer
explanation: Trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner; dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have a lamp on the left side as well.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: If a towed unit was manufactured before ABS was required and it's unclear whether it is equipped, how can a driver check?
choice_a: Check the color of the parking brake knob
choice_b: There is no way to determine this
choice_c: Test the alcohol evaporator
choice_d: Look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes
explanation: For towed units manufactured before ABS was required by the Department of Transportation, it may be difficult to tell if the unit has ABS; the driver should look under the vehicle for the electronic control unit (ECU) and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Does having ABS allow a driver to follow more closely or drive less carefully?
choice_a: Only in wet weather conditions
choice_b: No, ABS won't allow you to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully
choice_c: Yes, ABS is designed specifically to allow closer following distances
choice_d: Only on trailers, not on tractors
explanation: ABS won't allow a driver to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully; it only helps maintain control during hard braking when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.3.2, Braking with ABS

question: Before backing under a trailer, why should the fifth wheel plate be kept properly greased?
choice_a: Grease prevents the kingpin from bending
choice_b: Grease is only cosmetic and has no functional purpose
choice_c: Failure to keep it lubricated could cause steering problems from friction between the tractor and trailer
choice_d: It increases the governor cut-out pressure
explanation: As part of inspecting the fifth wheel before coupling, the driver must be sure the fifth wheel plate is greased as required, since failure to keep it lubricated could cause steering problems because of friction between the tractor and trailer.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 1)

question: When positioning the tractor to back under a trailer, why should the driver never back under the trailer at an angle?
choice_a: Doing so might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_b: It disables the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: It always damages the fifth wheel plate
choice_d: It is against Iowa's speed limit laws
explanation: The tractor should be put directly in front of the trailer; the driver should never back under the trailer at an angle, because doing so might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 3)

question: During coupling, how should the trailer height be adjusted relative to the tractor?
choice_a: The trailer should be low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when backed under it
choice_b: The trailer should always be higher than the fifth wheel to avoid contact
choice_c: The trailer should be lowered onto the ground before backing under
choice_d: Trailer height does not matter as long as the kingpin is present
explanation: The trailer should be low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when the tractor is backed under it; if too low, the tractor may strike and damage the trailer nose, and if too high, it may not couple correctly.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 6)

question: During the coupling process, why should the driver shut the engine off before applying and releasing the trailer brakes to check the connection?
choice_a: It automatically raises the landing gear
choice_b: It is required to prevent the tractor protection valve from popping out
choice_c: So the driver can hear the trailer brakes being applied and released, and air escaping when released
choice_d: To save fuel during the inspection
explanation: After supplying air to the trailer and waiting for normal air pressure, the driver shuts the engine off so they can hear the brakes; applying and releasing the trailer brakes should produce the sound of brakes moving when applied and air escaping when released.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 8)

question: Before backing the tractor under the trailer, what should the driver do with the air supply knob or tractor protection valve control?
choice_a: Push in the 'air supply' knob to release the trailer brakes
choice_b: Pull out the 'air supply' knob or move the control to 'emergency' to lock the trailer brakes
choice_c: Disconnect the control entirely
choice_d: Leave the control in whatever position it was left in previously
explanation: Before backing under the trailer, the driver pulls out the air supply knob or moves the tractor protection valve control from 'normal' to 'emergency' to lock the trailer brakes, then backs slowly under the trailer in the lowest reverse gear.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 9)

question: How does a driver check the connection for security after backing under the trailer and locking the kingpin?
choice_a: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked
choice_b: Disconnect the air lines and listen for hissing
choice_c: Immediately drive away at normal speed
choice_d: Check only that the electrical cord is plugged in
explanation: After stopping when the kingpin is locked into the fifth wheel, the driver raises the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pulls the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked, to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 11)

question: When inspecting the coupling, what does it mean if there is visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: It indicates the electrical cord is not connected
choice_b: This is normal and expected
choice_c: It means the landing gear needs to be lowered further
choice_d: Something is wrong; the kingpin may be sitting on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws, and the trailer could come loose very easily
explanation: The driver must make sure there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; if there is space, something is wrong, such as the kingpin resting on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws, meaning the trailer could come loose very easily.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 13)

question: Why should a driver never drive with the landing gear only part way up?
choice_a: It disables the trailer's turn signals
choice_b: It reduces fuel economy slightly
choice_c: It is only a cosmetic issue
choice_d: It may catch on railroad tracks or other things
explanation: The driver should raise the landing gear all the way up and never drive with landing gear only part way up, as it may catch on railroad tracks or other obstacles.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 15)

question: When uncoupling, why should a driver chock the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or the driver is unsure?
choice_a: It is only a recommendation with no real consequence
choice_b: It prevents the fifth wheel from rusting
choice_c: Air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing its emergency brakes, and without chocks the trailer could move
choice_d: Chocks are required only for legal liability reasons
explanation: The trailer wheels should be chocked if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or the driver isn't sure, because air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing its emergency brakes, and without chocks the trailer could then move.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 3)

question: When lowering the landing gear on a loaded trailer during uncoupling, why does the manual say to turn the crank a few extra turns after firm contact with the ground?
choice_a: To disconnect the air lines automatically
choice_b: To completely lift the trailer off the fifth wheel
choice_c: To lift some weight off the tractor, making it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and easier to couple next time
choice_d: It has no functional purpose, only tradition
explanation: After the landing gear makes firm contact with the ground on a loaded trailer, turning the crank a few extra turns in low gear lifts some weight off the tractor (without lifting the trailer off the fifth wheel), which makes it easier to unlatch the fifth wheel and easier to couple next time.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 4)

question: After disconnecting air lines from the trailer during uncoupling, what should the driver do with the air-line glad hands?
choice_a: Leave them open to drain remaining air
choice_b: Remove them from the tractor entirely
choice_c: Leave them hanging loose so they can drag on the ground
choice_d: Connect them to dummy couplers at the back of the cab or couple them together
explanation: When disconnecting the air-lines during uncoupling, the driver should connect the air-line glad hands to dummy couplers at the back of the cab or couple them together, keeping the electrical cable hung with plug down to keep moisture out.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 5)

question: After pulling the tractor forward until the fifth wheel clears the trailer, why should the driver stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer before continuing?
choice_a: It is required to reset the ABS system
choice_b: It allows the driver to check the oil level
choice_c: This prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink
choice_d: It has no safety purpose
explanation: After the fifth wheel comes out from under the trailer, the driver should stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer, which prevents the trailer from falling to the ground if the landing gear should collapse or sink.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers (Step 7)

question: According to the manual, what could result from failing to correctly lock the pintle hook latch?
choice_a: Only minor cosmetic damage to the hitch
choice_b: A brief delay in air pressure buildup
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp turning on
choice_d: Separation of the trailer and vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury
explanation: The manual warns that failure to correctly lock the pintle hook latch can result in separation of the trailer and vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.3, Coupling a Pintle Hook

question: What does the manual say is required by law for all trailers, regardless of hitch type?
choice_a: A pintle hook
choice_b: A trolley valve
choice_c: Safety chains
choice_d: A modulating control valve
explanation: When coupling a gooseneck hitch, the manual notes that all trailers are required by law to have safety chains, which must be attached during coupling.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.4.7, Coupling a Gooseneck Hitch (Step 3)

question: During a walk-around inspection of the fifth wheel, where should the locking jaws be positioned around the kingpin?
choice_a: Around the shank of the kingpin, not the head
choice_b: It does not matter as long as they are closed
choice_c: Around the head of the kingpin
choice_d: Below the kingpin entirely
explanation: During the walk-around inspection, the driver must check that the locking jaws are around the shank of the kingpin, not the head, and that the release arm is properly seated with the safety latch or lock engaged.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.1, Additional Things to Check during a Walk-around Inspection

question: When inspecting the landing gear on a combination vehicle, what should the driver confirm about the crank handle?
choice_a: It should be left loose for quick access
choice_b: It should be in place and secured
choice_c: It should be removed and stored separately
choice_d: It is not part of the landing gear inspection
explanation: As part of inspecting the landing gear, the driver checks that it is fully raised with no missing parts or damage, and that the crank handle is in place and secured.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.1, Additional Things to Check during a Walk-around Inspection (Landing Gear)

question: To check that air flows to all trailers, what should the driver do at the rear of the last trailer's emergency line shut-off valve?
choice_a: Open it and listen for air escaping, which shows the entire system is charged, then close it
choice_b: Leave it permanently open at all times
choice_c: Disconnect the glad hand instead of opening the valve
choice_d: Ignore it, since it is only relevant for the service line
explanation: After pushing in the red trailer air supply knob to supply air to the emergency lines, the driver goes to the rear of the rig and opens the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; hearing air escaping shows the entire system is charged, and the valve is then closed.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check (Check That Air Flows to All Trailers)

question: During the combination vehicle brake check, at about what air pressure range should the trailer air supply control (tractor protection valve control) pop out or move to 'emergency' as pressure is reduced?
choice_a: Usually within the range of 100 to 125 psi
choice_b: Usually within the range of 55 to 80 psi
choice_c: Usually within the range of 0 to 10 psi
choice_d: Usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi
explanation: To test the tractor protection valve, the driver charges the trailer air-brake system, shuts the engine off, and steps on and off the brake pedal to reduce air pressure; the trailer air supply control should pop out (or move from 'normal' to 'emergency') usually within the range of 20 to 45 psi, per the manufacturer's specification.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check (Test Tractor Protection Valve)

question: How does a driver test the trailer emergency brakes during the combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: By driving at highway speed and slamming on the brakes
choice_b: By charging the air system, checking the trailer rolls freely, then pulling out the trailer air supply control and pulling gently against the trailer with the tractor
choice_c: By disconnecting the electrical cord and observing the trailer lights
choice_d: By checking only the parking brake knob color
explanation: To test trailer emergency brakes, the driver charges the trailer air brake system, checks that the trailer rolls freely, then stops and pulls out the trailer air supply control (or places it in the 'emergency' position) and pulls gently on the trailer with the tractor to check the emergency brakes are on.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check (Test Trailer Emergency Brakes)

question: How does a driver test the trailer service brakes during the combination vehicle brake check?
choice_a: By observing the ABS malfunction lamp at start-up only
choice_b: By moving the vehicle forward slowly and applying the trailer brakes with the hand control (trolley valve) to feel them come on
choice_c: By pulling out the trailer air supply knob while parked
choice_d: By checking the alcohol evaporator fluid level
explanation: To test trailer service brakes, after checking for normal air pressure and releasing the parking brakes, the driver moves the vehicle forward slowly and applies the trailer brakes with the hand control (trolley valve); feeling the brakes come on confirms the trailer brakes are connected and working, though in normal operation they are controlled by the foot pedal.
source_note: Iowa Commercial Driver's License Manual (National CDL Manual, 2005 Testing System / 2017 Modernized Version, with Supplemental Sections 11 and 12; Iowa Department of Transportation) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check (Test Trailer Service Brakes)
